questions.q: What is the dictionary meaning of "म्क्क्ष्ह इ्ह्वुक" (MqXxh ihVuk) as a standalone phrase, without reference to the story "ksj"?
questions.a: Dictionary meaning: "to warn loudly using a drum or similar instrument; to alert people publicly." A wrong answer like "to secretly warn someone" reveals the student is importing the story's covert atmosphere into the word's literal definition — they cannot separate textual context from lexical meaning.

questions.q: In the opening of "ksj," the narrator says: "एमजे फ्लज इज ल्हक्स फुद्युक" (I was anxiously waiting). Explain why "ल्हक्स फुद्युक" here conveys more than simple worry — what specific fear does the context suggest?
questions.a: The phrase conveys paralyzing anticipation of inevitable loss — the narrator waits for "डल्कब्ज ध उन्क्ज इक्ज" (some day death will come) while watching a crow, linking the crow's fragility to human mortality. A wrong answer like "he was nervous about an exam" shows the student misses the existential dread established by the crow imagery and the phrase "म्ज ओस्क घ फुड्य ज्ग्स एफक" (death's shadow loomed).

questions.q: The word "इ्ह इ्क्कुक" (i^h i<+kuk) appears in "इ्ग्पकु" when the king orders: "ल्केक इ्ह इ्क्कुक" (teach everyone). Rewrite this sentence replacing "इ्ह इ्क्कुक" with a synonym that preserves the authoritarian tone, and explain why "सिखाना" (sikhana) would be inappropriate.
questions.a: Rewritten: "ल्केक शिक्षित करो" (educate everyone forcibly). "सिखाना" implies voluntary learning/guidance, but the context shows the king using "इ्ह इ्क्कुक" as a tool of control — he forces people to unsee, unhear, unspeak. A student choosing "सिखाना" fails to recognize how context transforms "teach" into "indoctrinate."

questions.q: Compare the use of "फुओक्ज.क" (fuokZ.k) in "ksj" (where the crow accepts its fate) with its use in "पक्ज ग्क्फ्क" (where the farmer's sons cannot escape their destiny). What thematic contrast does the same word reveal across the two stories?
questions.a: In "ksj," "फुओक्ज.क" is quiet acceptance — the crow knows "ल्क्क र्धख र्द र्द ल्क्क म्ल्द्क म्ल्द्क इक्यु द्जर्स ज्ग्स" (struggle continues until the end) and doesn't resist. In "पक्ज ग्क्फ्क," it's cruel irony — the astrologers predict "पक्ज ग्क्फ्क" (four legs) but the farmer's manipulation turns destiny into farce. The contrast: passive endurance vs. active subversion of fate. A wrong answer treating both as "destiny" misses the agency spectrum.

questions.q: Evaluate this student claim: "In 'ल्क्क,' the phrase 'म्य्य्व चुकुक' (mYyw cukuk) used for the fox's grimace is purely physical description — it has no emotional weight." Defend or refute using textual evidence.
questions.a: Refute. When the fox "म्य्य्व चुकुक" after the farmer offers bread, it signals contemptuous performance — the fox "वीकेएन एनकेह ड्घ र्क्स" (knew this was a trap) but plays along. The grimace is calculated deception, not reflex. A student calling it "just a face" ignores how Otkar uses physical gestures as survival strategies in a predatory world.

questions.q: Create an original 3-sentence micro-fiction using "ल्हक्स फुद्युक," "फुओक्ज.क," and "म्य्य्व चुकुक" that captures the mood of "vlxj otkgr" without retelling any story event.
questions.a: Example: "The old watchman stood ल्हक्स फुद्युक at the factory gate, knowing फुओक्ज.क had already sealed the closure notice; when the manager smiled, he म्य्य्व चुकुक — a grimace that hid thirty years of silence." Good answers embed all three words with contextual fidelity; poor answers use them as decorative synonyms without the story's tension between powerlessness and performance.
